title: I/We/You: Use with Caution
author: Rachel Ball and Alex Fairlamb
summary: Rachel Ball and Alex Fairlamb, drawing on research for their forthcoming book The Scaffolding Effect, warn that the I/We/You gradual-release framework - powerful as a way to conceptualise a teaching sequence - is at serious risk of 'lethal mutation' when schools convert it into a rigid, timed lesson structure. They report teachers being told to reach the independent 'you do' phase by a specific time, checked by classroom observers, which strips out the responsiveness the model was designed to enable. The authors give four reasons the rigid version fails: I/We/You is properly a flexible continuum (per Quigley, 2022) rather than a fixed sequence, and real lessons often cycle through I/We/We/I/We/You multiple times based on checks for understanding; enforcing a fixed structure removes teacher agency to adapt in response to student feedback; different subjects need the cycle at very different paces (rapid cycles in maths versus multi-week independent art projects); and I/We/You, on its own, doesn't incorporate other essential elements like retrieval, prior-knowledge activation, or whole-class feedback. Their conclusion affirms the underlying model's value while insisting it must remain adaptive: used as a rigid, branded, compliance-driven structure, it produces worse teaching and demoralised staff, not more consistency.
points: Ball and Fairlamb's central warning: I/We/You is 'a powerful way to plan and execute a learning cycle' but becomes 'painfully flawed' when enforced as a rigid, timed lesson structure rather than treated as a flexible continuum.
They report a concrete symptom of this mutation: teachers told they must be 'on' the independent 'you do' phase by a specific time in the lesson, with compliance checked by classroom observers.

Reason 2 in their argument - teacher agency: a mandated I/We/You structure prevents teachers from adapting instruction in response to real-time checks for understanding, effectively asking them to ignore evidence that students aren't ready to move on.

Reason 3 - subject variation: I/We/You cycles can take seconds in maths (e.g., quick worked examples before independent practice) but unfold over weeks in subjects like GCSE Art, where a single mandated lesson structure makes no sense.

Reason 4 - incompleteness: I/We/You on its own doesn't explicitly build in retrieval practice, activation of prior learning, or whole-class feedback, so treating it as the entire lesson-planning framework risks crowding out those other essential elements.
quotes: 'To me, I/We/You is a powerful way to conceptualise teaching specific things. It is NOT a powerful way to structure lessons. It's a cycle. And you could have multiple cycles in any given 55 minute lesson.'
Worryingly, teachers have anecdotally shared with us that they have been told to be 'on' the 'you do' phase of the lesson at a certain time, checked by observers.
It's our aim here therefore, to remind leaders to be vigilant, and forewarn that 'I/We/You' is vulnerable to lethal mutation.
Having a prescriptive lesson structure of I/We/You prevents the teacher from exercising their professional expertise to adapt the teaching in light of student feedback.
Generic, top-down strategies quite often ignore the beautiful nuances of individual subjects and lead to a 'one-size-fits-all' approach.
However, as a longer term teaching and learning strategy, it will straightjacket teacher agency to be adaptive and deploy different aspects of their toolkit when appropriate to.
